title: Establish the physical energy budget of coronal heating

concept.text: The innovation would be a quantitatively verified explanation of how energy reaches the Sun’s corona, moves through it and becomes heat. Establishing that physical energy budget means accounting for the energy supplied, transported, converted and lost, while explaining the observed coronal conditions. Identifying an energetic event or showing that a mechanism can produce heating would contribute to this goal; the larger advance would connect those processes into a predictive physical account.

The account must distinguish magnetically open regions from closed regions, where magnetic structures connect back to the Sun. Different environments may receive different contributions from waves and small magnetic reconnection events. These processes can also interact: reconnection can generate waves, and waves can trigger reconnection. A successful explanation therefore need not identify one universal heating mechanism; it could establish how several coupled mechanisms contribute under different conditions.

significance.text: A verified energy budget would resolve a longstanding problem in astrophysical plasma physics by turning incompletely constrained explanations into a physical account that makes testable predictions. Its scientific importance would lie in explaining which energy pathways sustain different coronal environments, how much each contributes and why their relative importance changes. That would provide a stronger foundation for models of solar spectral irradiance and the connection between magnetic activity and emitted radiation.

The Sun would then provide a better constrained basis for investigating other stellar coronae and their spectral irradiance. This extension would remain conditional: a model validated in solar environments would still need tests under other stellar conditions. Improvements in operational space-weather prediction could also follow, but would require additional observations and forecasting advances. Closing the heating budget alone would not establish reliable forecasts of individual space-weather events.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is to trace and quantify the relevant energy transfers across coronal environments well enough to determine their relative contributions. The September 2022 white paper describes unresolved questions about wave heating and reconnection, including their importance in the quiet Sun. Because the processes can be coupled and impulsive, a model must explain the physical sequence of energy conversion rather than merely reproduce an observed temperature or brightness using an assumed heating input.

Concrete barriers include thin dissipation layers, unresolved magnetic strands, rapid energy-release episodes and interactions between spatial scales. The decisive regions may be too small or too short-lived to measure directly with available diagnostics. Progress therefore requires coordinated observations and models that constrain these hidden transfers while preserving the physical flow from magnetic energy through motions to thermal energy. Complementary diagnostics are needed because a single observable or instrument cannot necessarily distinguish competing pathways.

Reconnection-associated particle acceleration presents a further interpretive distinction. Evidence that particles gain energy during reconnection establishes an energy-conversion process in the measured setting. Establishing coronal heating additionally requires determining how much energy becomes thermal energy, where it is deposited and whether the resulting contribution accounts for the relevant heating requirement alongside other processes. The supplied Parker Solar Probe report does not itself supply that broader accounting.

current_state.text: In their September 7, 2022 white paper, “Heating of the Magnetically Closed Corona and Physical Models of Solar and Stellar Spectral Irradiances,” James A. Klimchuk and colleagues described unresolved questions about the mechanisms and relative contributions of coronal heating. They distinguished open and closed magnetic environments, discussed potentially coupled wave and reconnection heating, and credited Parker Solar Probe with valuable information. The document emphasizes the closed corona; its discussion of open regions does not constitute a comprehensive demonstrated budget for both environments.

Southwest Research Institute’s June 3, 2025 press release reported Parker Solar Probe observations of particle energization associated with magnetic reconnection at the near-Sun heliospheric current sheet. It described a sunward-directed reconnection jet and sunward-propagating highly energetic protons. This is relevant observational progress on energy conversion in the nascent solar wind. Its scope is a particular reconnection environment; the reported observations do not establish the thermal heating budget across open and closed coronal regions.

The supplied review identifies complete retained text for the 2022 white paper and the 2025 press release, but the research paper associated with the press release is absent from the supplied evidence. Consequently, the observational description here rests on the institutional report and cannot be extended into a paper-level assessment of quantitative energy closure. The unrelated employment documents downloaded alongside that report provide no scientific corroboration, but their presence does not invalidate the report.

Evidence boundary: these dated sources establish historical discussion and reported observational progress. The supplied record contains no freshness assessment establishing the complete state of the field as of November 1, 2026. It therefore does not determine whether subsequent work has closed additional parts of the budget or achieved the broader proposed breakthrough. That limitation leaves the later field-wide position uncertain; it is not evidence that the reported observations are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: coordinated measurements and physically faithful models should resolve or otherwise constrain energy inputs, transport, conversion and losses sufficiently to close the heating budget across a declared set of representative open and closed coronal environments. Each case should report the accounting uncertainty and the range of contributions still allowed for competing or coupled mechanisms. These are proposed criteria grounded in the documented energy-flow problem, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: Close heating budgets across representative open and closed coronal environments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: the investigators should specify representative environments, validation observables and acceptable closure uncertainties before evaluating the result. Predictions should then be tested against observations outside the cases used to fit the model, using complementary diagnostics where possible. Reproducing an observed brightness or temperature should be accompanied by evidence that the modeled energy pathway is physically consistent with the measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Validate physically consistent energy pathways against observations outside model-fitting cases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent analyses should recover compatible budgets from documented measurements and modeling assumptions, with uncertainty propagated through the accounting. The demonstration should distinguish energy deposited as heat from energy carried by accelerated particles or other channels, and should identify unresolved transfers that could materially change the result. Success would establish the explanation’s demonstrated breadth across the tested conditions. Finite tests would not prove literal universality, and extension to untested solar environments or other stars would require further validation.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduce compatible energy budgets with propagated accounting uncertainty

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: AST-11, “Identify the first generation of metal-free stars,” is related through stellar physics, but asks which early stellar populations existed; AST-14 asks how energy heats stellar outer atmospheres, beginning with the Sun. AST-13, “Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew,” shares an interest in physical energy processes but targets the formation and evolution of a different class of astronomical object. Neither objective is established by a coronal heating solution.

Roster synthesis: AST-01, “Establish that an exoplanet hosts life,” and AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” have an indirect connection through the stellar environments of planets. Better physical models of stellar radiation could contribute context for interpreting planetary observations, subject to validation beyond the Sun. Coronal energy-budget closure would itself establish neither life nor a resolved planetary surface map.

Roster synthesis: AST-09, “Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources,” and AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory,” concern observational capabilities with different signals and targets. AST-14 instead concerns a quantitative physical explanation that must be tested through observations and modeling. Its overlap with magnetic reconnection, turbulence, plasma physics and space weather describes contributing disciplines and possible applications; those topics are not separate entries in the supplied roster.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the complete state of coronal heating research as of November 1, 2026; subsequent progress remains unassessed.
The research paper associated with the June 3, 2025 SwRI release is absent, leaving its detailed methods, quantitative energy accounting and uncertainties unavailable for assessment here.
Representative environments, validation observables, acceptable closure uncertainties and reproducibility tolerances remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.
The relative contributions of coupled heating mechanisms and the conditions governing their importance are not quantitatively resolved by the supplied sources.
The range of stellar conditions over which a future solar heating account could be generalized remains to be demonstrated.

brief.title: An explanation of what heats the Sun’s outer atmosphere
possible: We could explain how the Sun keeps its outer atmosphere, called the corona, so much hotter than its surface. Scientists could trace the energy from its source through to heat and account for what escapes.

That explanation would cover both open regions, where magnetic fields extend into space, and closed regions, where they loop back to the Sun. It would establish how much each heating process contributes in different settings.
why: Scientists would gain a physical explanation that makes testable predictions about the Sun’s radiation. This would strengthen models of how magnetic activity produces ultraviolet light and X-rays, which affect Earth’s upper atmosphere.
The Sun would also become a better starting point for studying the hot atmospheres of other stars and the radiation they emit.

sources.showed: Their white paper sets out a strategy for explaining heating in closed regions. It describes how waves and magnetic reconnection—the breaking and rejoining of magnetic field lines—can interact, and why tiny energy-release sites challenge models.
sources.cited_for: It explains the competing heating processes and the need to follow the physical flow of energy.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a complete energy budget across open and closed regions.

sources.who: Mihir Desai and a Southwest Research Institute-led team
sources.showed: The team reported Parker Solar Probe observations linking energetic particles near the Sun to magnetic reconnection. The spacecraft detected a jet and energetic protons moving toward the Sun.
sources.quote: Within the core of the reconnection exhaust, Parker detected trapped energetic protons a thousand times greater than the available magnetic energy per particle.
sources.cited_for: The observations connect magnetic reconnection with particle energization near the Sun.
sources.not_established: Particle acceleration does not establish how much energy becomes heat or whether it meets the corona’s heating needs.

shown: A Southwest Research Institute-led team has linked energetic particles near the Sun to magnetic reconnection using Parker Solar Probe measurements. This establishes an energy-conversion process in a particular setting.

Klimchuk and colleagues describe how waves and reconnection could sustain closed regions. Their account explains why matching the Sun’s temperature or brightness alone cannot establish that a model gets the heating process right.
missing: Measurements and models must account for energy entering, moving through, heating and leaving representative open and closed regions.
The contributions of waves and reconnection must be separated or constrained, including where they interact.
Tiny, brief energy transfers must be constrained well enough to distinguish heat from energy carried away by accelerated particles.

milestones.label: Complete energy budgets across open and closed regions
milestones.explanation: Measurements and models would have to account for energy inputs, transfers, heating and losses across representative regions, with stated uncertainties. This would establish how much each process can contribute.

milestones.label: Successful predictions beyond the cases used to fit models
milestones.explanation: Models would have to predict separate observations under criteria set beforehand, with measurements supporting the proposed energy pathways. This would test whether the explanation holds beyond its fitting cases.

milestones.label: Independent agreement on energy budgets and their uncertainties
milestones.explanation: Independent analyses would have to recover compatible budgets, carrying uncertainties through the accounting and distinguishing heat from other energy channels. This would establish reproducibility across the tested conditions.

uncertain: Which environments and measurements would provide a representative test, and how much accounting uncertainty would be acceptable?
How do the relative contributions of waves and reconnection change across solar conditions?
How far could an explanation tested on the Sun extend to other stars?

page.title: Energy budget of solar coronal heating
page.definition: A physical account of how energy reaches the Sun’s corona, its outer atmosphere, and becomes heat, with measured inputs and losses reconciled. It covers open magnetic fields extending into space and closed fields returning to the Sun.

goal.need: The corona reaches roughly 1–2 million K above a photosphere near 5,770 K. Maintaining it requires replacing energy lost through radiation, conduction and outflow. Published heating requirements differ by more than a factor of 30 across coronal environments. Identifying an energy reservoir therefore leaves the physical problem of transporting and converting its energy into the required heat.

completion.title: A physical energy budget accounts for heating in open and closed solar coronal regions.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed physical account quantitatively constrains the heating pathways in open and closed coronal regions. Inputs, changes in stored energy, and radiative, conductive and outflow losses balance within reported observational uncertainties. The inferred heat deposition reproduces measured plasma properties and radiation, with energy retained in nonthermal particles distinguished from heat. Dissipation follows physically justified coronal processes rather than an independently adjustable heating function.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published coronal-heating requirements; no external integrated acceptance test was found.
completion.basis: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe goals, the 2025 decadal-survey panel report, DKIST’s Critical Science Plan and coronal-heating reviews were searched. They require energy tracing, physical conversion and observational tests, but define no agreed completion test spanning open and closed regions or numerical closure tolerance. This test combines those requirements without assigning a percentage tolerance.

milestones.title: An identified energy source supplies at least the power lost by a coronal region.
milestones.criterion: Identify a source whose available power equals or exceeds the losses of the specified coronal environment. Closed: Klimchuk’s 2006 estimates find magnetic stressing sufficient for quiet-Sun and active-region losses when horizontal and vertical fields are comparable. Open: Rivera et al. find wave energy sufficient for heating and acceleration in one stream measured on 25 February 2022 and 27 February 2022, between 13.3 and 127.7 solar radii; this tests the outer-corona–heliosphere interval.
milestones.set_by: Coronal-heating energy-supply criterion in Klimchuk (2006), section 2; its staged framework is also used by Reale (2014). The quoted formulation concerns closed regions.
milestones.threshold_quote: an energy source that can sustain these levels of losses.

milestones.title: A coronal heating model converts source energy into heat through the physical dissipation pathway.
milestones.criterion: Quantify conversion into heat through a physically justified coronal dissipation pathway. Open: one Parker Solar Probe current-sheet crossing on 12 December 2022 at 16.25 solar radii produced protons up to about 400 keV, demonstrating particle acceleration without closing the thermal budget. Closed: Kuniyoshi and Morton’s model of one quiet-Sun loop attributes at least 80% of heating to Alfvén-wave turbulence. Posted on 15 August 2026 and accepted by ApJ, it uses numerical dissipation on a 60 km grid; the fraction is not fully converged.
milestones.set_by: Physical energy-conversion requirement in Klimchuk et al. (2022), page 3, and the distinction between wave damping and dissipation in Arregui (2015), section 4. The quoted requirement concerns closed regions.
milestones.threshold_quote: The flow of energy in the model must proceed as in the real corona

milestones.title: A coronal heating model reproduces the measured plasma and radiation of a specified region.
milestones.criterion: A model connects its heating to plasma response and synthetic radiation that agrees quantitatively with observations. Closed: Yang et al. reproduce emission-measure and extreme-ultraviolet intensity distributions for one active region, NOAA 11416, on 11 February 2012, with one fitted global parameter. Open and closed: AWSoM compares synthetic extreme-ultraviolet emission with observations on 7 March 2011 for one Carrington rotation, CR2107. Its wave dissipation is parameterized; these comparisons do not establish the full physical budget.
milestones.set_by: Coronal-heating forward-modeling test in Klimchuk (2006), sections 1, 5 and 6, also described by Reale (2014). Quantitative observational comparisons are applied by Yang et al. (2018) and van der Holst et al. (2014). Klimchuk’s formulation concerns closed regions.
milestones.threshold_quote: a prediction of observable quantities that can be compared directly with actual observations.

not_found: No agreed numerical closure tolerance or required set of coronal environments was found in the mission goals, science plans, decadal survey or reviews searched.

results.finding: One current-sheet crossing detected trapped energetic protons at 1,000 times the available magnetic energy per particle.
results.detail: The observations connect magnetic reconnection to particle acceleration, but do not quantify conversion into heat or close the thermal energy budget.

results.finding: In one polar coronal hole, four observations yielded an Alfvén-wave energy flux of 6.7 ± 0.7 × 10⁵ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹.
results.detail: The estimated energy requirement was approximately 6 × 10⁵ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ during the 2007–2009 solar minimum. The analysis assumes constant ion temperatures and undamped waves at low heights.
results.quote: We have found that Alfvén waves in a polar coronal hole possess sufficient energy to heat the coronal hole and that this energy is actually dissipated from the waves at sufficiently low heights to heat the corona.

results.finding: In one fast solar-wind stream, Alfvén waves dissipated an estimated 3.9 ± 2.9 W/m², enough for heating and acceleration.
results.detail: The estimated heating and acceleration requirement was 3.62 ± 0.40 W/m². The comparison covers 13.3–127.7 solar radii and relies on stream matching and a modeled heating profile; the estimates have substantial uncertainty.
results.quote: Our calculations show the damping and mechanical work performed by the Alfvén waves is sufficient to power the heating and acceleration of the fast solar wind in the inner heliosphere.

results.finding: In one simulated quiet-Sun coronal loop, Alfvén-wave turbulence accounts for at least 80% of coronal heating.
results.detail: The simulation uses numerical dissipation on a 60 km grid. The reported heating fraction is not fully converged.

results.finding: In one coronal-hole-connected stream, empirical proton heating peaked at 1.1 times the perpendicular thermal speed.
results.detail: The inferred heating profile agrees with a stochastic-heating model that includes intermittent fluctuations. The reported comparison is normalized, and the text gives no absolute heating rate or quantitative energy conversion from the source.
results.quote: We show evidence for a Fokker-Planck type diffusive process in the sub-Alfvénic stream of study, and that scale-dependent SH rates, which include intermittency, match our empirical measurements both in magnitude, and in the region of phase space where these heating rates peak.

results.finding: Across 7,831 PSP intervals, intermittent stochastic heating approximately matches local energy transfer below 15 solar radii.
results.detail: The sample includes both sub- and super-Alfvénic wind. Heating rates are model estimates; the comparison depends on assumed coefficients and does not close the total thermal budget.

results.finding: Yang et al. reproduce emission-measure and EUV intensity distributions for 1 active region, NOAA 11416, with 1 global free parameter.
results.detail: The model assumes equilibrium loops and a 160 km reconnection scale; the fitted heating scale parameter is approximately 0.3. The highest-temperature emission measures retain a discrepancy.
results.quote: The predicted thermal structure of the corona, in particular the DEM and intensity distributions, resemble the observations both qualitatively and quantitatively.

results.finding: For one equatorial coronal region, AWSoM line widths for 5 ions differed from observations by less than 10% at most heights.
results.detail: The global model includes open and closed fields, but the text does not establish that the measured emission came specifically from open field. Synthetic fluxes for three of five ions were underestimated, and the comparison concerns CR1916 rather than CR2107.
results.quote: The first thing we note is that the ratios for all lines are all very close to unity, with a discrepancy of less than 10% at most heights.
